title: ECP5 bitstream problem with --spimode
body:
The recent PR #588  to add spimode as a parameter breaks the bitstreams for my color light 5A-75E when programmed using an FT2232 and openFPGALoader. The bitstreams being produced by ecppack when the --spimode flag is specified cannot be programmed by openFPGALoader. Here is the very trimmed down sequence of events.

```
build$ ecppack top.config --svf top.svf --bit top.bit --bootaddr 0 --spimode fast-read
build$ openFPGALoader -c ft2232 top.bit
Open file top.bit DONE
Parse file DONE
Enable configuration: DONE
SRAM erase: DONE
Loading: [==================================================] 100.000000%
Fail
displayReadReg
        Config Target Selection : 0
        JTAG Active
        ISC Enable
        Write Enable
        Read Enable
        Abort ERR
        EXEC Error
build$ ecppack top.config --svf top.svf --bit top.bit --bootaddr 0
build$ openFPGALoader -c ft2232 top.bit
Open file top.bit DONE
Parse file DONE
Enable configuration: DONE
SRAM erase: DONE
Loading: [==================================================] 100.000000%
Done
Disable configuration: DONE

```

The second run of ecppack, without the --spimode flag, produces a bitstream which can be programmed. The first run is consistently broken.

I realize that this is almost certainly an ecppack issue but the changes here to use --spimode triggered it for me so maybe someone else sees it and has an idea. I will submit an issue for ecppack.

fix_commits.messageHeadline: build/lattice/trellis: set default spimode to None (--spimode not pas…

comments.body:
Ecppack puts "0x79 0x49 0x00 0x00" into the bitstream when --spimode fast-read is set.  dual-spi spimode adds "0x79 0x51 0x00 0x00" and qspi adds "0x79 0x59 0x00 0x00".

When the --spimode flag is omitted then this sequence is omitted completely.

My 5A-75E flash chip doesn't like any of the above spimode options so I would need to be able to omit the spimode flag. Perhaps it could default to nothing instead of fast-read. It begins to look like it isn't really an ecppack issue after all.

OK, a last comment. If I use

`openFPGALoader -c ft2232 -f top.bit`

to write the bitstream to flash then the bitstream produced by --spimode fast-read works! My flash chip does like the fast-read mode after all.

I guess the bottom line is that bitstreams created with spimode options cannot be used for SRAM uploads.

Yes, that is correct, the SPI mode flags break uploads via JTAG or other SRAM programming routes. prjtrellis actually strips them automagically when creating an svf file, but that doesn't help when creating a bit file for another programming tool.

Thanks @derekmulcahy, @daveshah1, with https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/6671eb6218ce35a4b79f3c6dbbb2092bcaa3b41f spimode is set to None by default (and --spimode is not passed to ecppack in this case).
Awesome! Fixed while I slept!

For people like me looking for a solution to the problem, an easy solution is to edit `micropython/ports/litex/Makefile` :

```
$(Q)$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -o $@ $^ $(LIBS)
```

to be replaced with

```mk
$(Q)$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -march=rv32i -o $@ $^ $(LIBS)
```

The reason is that `newlib` in my toolchain only supports the following targets:

```bash
$ ls /usr/lib/gcc/riscv64-elf/12.2.0/rv*
rv32i/      rv32im/     rv32imafc/  rv64imafdc/ 
rv32iac/    rv32imac/   rv64imac/
```
but as suarezvictor says it is set to `-march=rv32i2p0`.

Also, if you need LTO, replace it with:

```
$(Q)$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -march=rv32i -misa-spec=2.2 -o $@ $^ $(LIBS)
```

title: License update makes LiteX non-free
body:
The recent updates to the license make LiteX non-free with respect to the OSI definition.
Also these additions mean that corporate legal teams would not accept the usage of LiteX.

I don't know if this is an intended consequence, and if so, its a bug.

I'd also check that all license holders agree with the license change if this is intended, as this is now a narrower license than BSD 2-Clause.

```
Conditions: The project is shared with a permissive BSD 2-Clause License and we
are encouraged to continue sharing it this way thanks to the awesome community
and clients willing to support the project!

To be able to continue doing so, in addition of the BSD 2-Clause License conditions,
we are expecting users to behave with integrity:
- Users making useful use of the project have to be coherent in their behaviour
on social networks.
- Clients using it for commercial use and with unpaid invoices (due to bankruptcy,
liquidation or dissagrements) are not allowed to use/re-integrate post-conflict
developments unless they want to discuss/regularize the situation.
```

fix_commits.messageHeadline: LICENSE: Move moral precisions to README.md to be OSI compliant and r…

comments.body:
Fixed with https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/db87fa1a7f91757b52be9d2740fee75906f0e959, intent was not to change the licensing but just to add some precision on our expectation regarding users/clients' behavior. I moved this to the README.md and rephrased it a bit.

It's sad to have to add such precision since I was expecting this to be implicit and it's clearly the case for 99% of users/clients  playing the game, but it seems to be required for the remaining 1%.

The intent of the project is to share as much development as possible in the LiteX ecosystem and encourage our partners/clients to do the same while putting accents on the advantage of open-sourcing things (benefit from future features, reduce maintenance, contribute a piece and enable others to build upon, etc...) The LiteX ecosystem does not has a private side, we only have private designs build with it for clients and are always trying to convince clients to make non project specific parts open-source (Which is not an easy task). More and more developers/clients/partners are playing the game, which is encouraging since this is not yet a common approach in hardware development.  To be able to continue in this direction and put priority on technology rather than business or just stop sharing some of the development, this precision seems useful.

Thanks for your understanding,

Florent

title: Zynq address decoding issue
body:
While working on a target using Zynq7000 cpu I stumbled upon a problem with decoding the address space / selecting suitable bus to perform operation on CSRs.
I’m trying to add a single non-LiteX peripheral to a Zynq7000 SoC, behind AXI2Wishbone bridge of base address `0x43c0 0000`. The peripheral is connected via wishbone bus that follows to the core’s decoder, where the control is delegated further. It also provides two AXI slaves and these are too connected in the target but they’re not the focus of the problem.
From what I’ve been able to trace back there were some changes made regarding the `csr_decode` property in Zynq7000 with commit [f46d1c1](https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/f46d1c190b9dc87ecfea43def69862ce99d99559). And I do understand it was introduced in order to be able to decode the addresses correctly while using the bridge, however, disabling the decoding SoCRegion in Zynq7000 seems to cause an issue where the `csr_bridge` the LiteX is placing (while finalizing the SoC) is always selected. Therefore, always being granted access to the data channel. I.e. rdata for Zynq7000.

```
always @(*) begin                          	 
	slave_sel <= 2'd0;                     	 
	slave_sel[0] <= (shared_adr[29:15] == 1'd0);
	slave_sel[1] <= 1'd1;                  	 
end 
```
                                       	 
Where then `slave_sel` is assigned to `slave_sel_r`.
```
always @(*) begin                                                                                            	 
	(..)
	shared_dat_r <= (({32{slave_sel_r[0]}} & wb_control_dat_r) | ({32{slave_sel_r[1]}} & basesoc_wishbone_dat_r));
```

Where `wb_control_dat_r` is assigned to my core’s `dat_o` and the `basesoc_wishbone_dat_r` is from various data sources generated by LiteX infrastructure.
When simply enabling default decoding in `Zynq7000` cpu in target:
```
self.cpu.csr_decode = True
```
The generated verilog changes to:
```
always @(*) begin                               	 
	slave_sel <= 2'd0;                          	 
	slave_sel[0] <= (shared_adr[29:15] == 1'd0);	 
	slave_sel[1] <= (shared_adr[29:14] == 15'd17344);
end                       
```                      	 
(the rest stays the same)
In which case, the data passed by my core doesn’t get or’ed with the data passed from base soc.
Now, the way I constructed my target is I placed the bridge at `0x43c0 0000` and I placed my core at the `SoCRegion` of origin 0x0, this way it’s address is properly decoded even if zynq's  `csr_decode = True`.
I don’t know why exactly changing the decoding in zynq impacts the selection this greatly. Looks like it got optimised this way.

fix_commits.messageHeadline: integration/soc/SoCBusHandler: Force interconnect to Crossbar when at…

comments.body:
Hi @kgugala,

sorry for the delay. This should be "fixed" with https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/b367c27191511f36b10ec4103198978f86f9502c:
- The CSR decoding is reverted (so has to be handled in software).
- The build will now fail if such condition occur (More than one Region with one of them with no decoder).

This should already be addressed in current LiteX.

The problematic behavior came from disabling CSR decoding on Zynq, which could make the LiteX CSR bridge decode too broadly and get selected together with another region. This was corrected with:

enjoy-digital/litex@b367c27191511f36b10ec4103198978f86f9502c

Current LiteX keeps CSR decoding enabled for Zynq/ZynqMP, since the AXI address is decoded in the AXI2Wishbone bridge and the offset has to be handled in software. LiteX also now rejects ambiguous bus  maps where more than one region exists and one of them has decoding disabled, instead of silently generating an unsafe decoder.

So I think this can be closed. If there is still a current reproducer on master, please share the target/configuration and generated bus map so we can look at that specific case.

comments.body:
Hi,

I attempted to reproduce this issue while investigating the LiteX + VexiiRiscv Linux boot flow.

Environment I used:

* LiteX (latest master)
* VexiiRiscv (latest)
* riscv64-unknown-elf toolchain
* Linux build targeting VexiiRiscv
* Host: WSL Ubuntu

While setting up the environment I noticed that several build scripts and generated paths may still reference Windows-mounted paths (e.g. `/mnt/c/...`) when building under WSL. This can sometimes lead to inconsistent execution of scripts during the software build phase (picolibc / BIOS generation).

Because of this, I am currently rebuilding the environment fully inside the Linux filesystem (`~/litex`) to eliminate potential WSL filesystem issues.

So far I have observed that the boot log proceeds normally through:

* SMP initialization
* memory initialization
* devtmpfs setup
* NETLINK registration
* SBI misaligned access delegation

and then stops after:

`SBI misaligned access exception delegation ok`

This suggests the system may already be transitioning into later kernel initialization stages when the hang occurs.

I am still working on reproducing the issue consistently and will share additional observations once I can run the full Linux boot with the same configuration (`--cpu-type vexiiriscv --cpu-variant debian`).

If anyone has additional debug logs (especially with earlycon or additional kernel debug flags), that might help narrow down where the kernel stops progressing.

Thanks.

I had the exactly the same problem myself.
The issue occurs in the Linux Kernel `arch -> riscv -> kernel -> unaligned_access.speed.c` within the function `check_unaligned_access()`. There is a while loop that pauses as long as the jiffies remain the same: `while ((now = jiffies) == start_jiffies)`, and the problem is that it gets stuck there.
My solution was to add the following lines to `linux.config` (VexiiRiscv->doc->litex->buildroot->board->litex_soc): 
```
# Disable Misaligned
CONFIG_RISCV_MISALIGNED=n
CONFIG_RISCV_PROBE_UNALIGNED_ACCESS=n
```

Hope this helps.
Best regards, Alex

@KunoTV 
It works, thanks for your help!!!!

However, it still gets stuck there for about 10 seconds. Previously, when I booted Linux, I didn’t need to set this option, and there was no such delay. 
Maybe there is a new issue with the hardware?

Hi @looongbin,

thanks for the report. I'll try to have a look. Do you know when was built your last booting bitstream?

Hi @enjoy-digital,
About February 12th, I hadn’t encountered this issue when compiling with the latest branch prior to that date.
Thanks for your help!
Thanks @looongbin, I'll investigate. If you don't mind, can you also share your target? (in case the issue is specific to it).

@enjoy-digital , files of my board in litex-boards. Wish it helps.
https://github.com/looongbin/litex-boards/commit/2258ff3db49c13c1375dc8780897cf97f923fe7a

Hi, @enjoy-digital, @looongbin, @KunoTV . I have found the fault I have caused and add a fix for it.

The reason is pretty simple, the litex always gives `--imsic-interrupt-number=0` argument to VexiiRiscv, this will add Ssaia extension, which will change the generation path to AIA logic. Also I have also make a mistake for a wrong interrupt id. This two give a wrong result for the hardware generation, as kernel can not enable time interrupt. So the system is halted.

I have opened a PR for a fix. I think a version bump is needed to close this problem after @Dolu1990 merge the PR in VexiiRiscv.

@inochisa Thanks for the fix ^^
Merge vexiiriscv done, Litex PR https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/pull/2449

title: soc/software/bios: The linker script breaks linkage with `--build-id` flag
body:
After running LiteDRAM's `test_examples.py` tests it turned out there's a linkage problem when GCC is configured with `--enable-linker-build-id` which makes it pass the `--build-id` flag to a linker. Using that option with current BIOS linker scripts ends up in such an error:
```
  <PATH>/ld.bfd.real: section .note.gnu.build-id LMA [0000000000000000,0000000000000023] overlaps section .text LMA [0000000000000000,0000000000005333]
  collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
  make: *** [<PATH>/litex/soc/software/bios/Makefile:60: bios.elf] Error 1
```

fix_commits.messageHeadline: bios: mark .note.gnu.build-id as non-loadable but don't disable it
bios: mark .note.gnu.build-id as non-loadable but don't disable it

comments.body: CC @danc86
@shenki - You were doing something here right?
Might be related to https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/pull/1020 ?

The testing was indeed conducted with an older LiteX revision (https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/ab9f214a5ee4ab5bf96e19ff3520cf59092ad11a) so there should be no such error after that change. Passing `--build-id=none` prohibits a linker from adding the `build-id`.

Sorry for not testing the latest revision before creating this issue. I'll let you know after I check if this change is enough.
As expected, the BIOS is buildable after making such a change in `common.mak`. Still, I'll leave closing the issue to @danc86 as he might want to add something to it.

Thanks @ajelinski.

I don't think overriding `--build-id` to turn it off is the best approach, if the environment has explicitly requested it. Distros like Chrome OS generally want to inject a build id and expect that the resulting ELF executable will have the `.note.gnu.build-id` section, so that their debuginfo processing can do stuff with it.

More generally, non-loadable `.note` sections are used for injecting various other kinds of metadata into the executable, like Fedora's [annobin plugin](https://developers.redhat.com/blog/2018/02/20/annobin-storing-information-binaries#how_to_use_it). And DWARF debug sections fall into this category too, they are extra metadata kept in the ELF output even though they will not be included in the final firmware image.

The issue with `--build-id` seems to just be that the `.note.gnu.build-id` section is marked *loadable*, unlike the other kinds of metadata sections. As far as I can tell, this is done so that programs can extract their own build id at runtime. I even found [a blog post](https://interrupt.memfault.com/blog/gnu-build-id-for-firmware) about using it in embedded firmware to identify the version of code running, which is an interesting idea.

But since the Litex BIOS can't use the build id at runtime I would suggest to just mark it non-loadable in the linker script, so that it's kept in the ELF but doesn't cause an error by overlapping with .text and won't be copied to the final `bios.bin` image. I've sent PR #1044 for that.

Either way, the issue with `--build-id` doesn't happen with the latest `master` branch so we can definitely close this issue.
@shenki - Thoughts?
I'm closing the issue since the problem is fixed and the change proposed by @danc86 has its own PR where it can be discussed.

```bash

```
After a few seconds, got stuck with:
```bash

(Litex 2022.08)

Hello, it seems that I've managed to find a reason for this failure - I generated VCD traces for the litex simulation, analyzed them in gtkwave and here is what I found.

This is a part of disassembled `bios.bin`:
```
0000254c <litex_putc>:
   ...
   ...
    2562:	37ed                	jal	254c <litex_putc>
    2564:	40b2                	lw	ra,12(sp)
    2566:	8522                	mv	a0,s0
    2568:	4422                	lw	s0,8(sp)
    256a:	0141                	addi	sp,sp,16
    256c:	8082                	ret
```
During execution of this part of code a strange bug happens - at some point the CPU is executing `jal` instruction, but for some reason it saves 2566 as a return address instead of 2564. This results in omitting ` lw    ra,12(sp)`  instruction after we return from the function call. This `lw` instruction is responsible for restoring the return address of the caller function, but since it is not executed, the 2566 value is still left in `ra` register. Therefore, executing `ret` later on results in jumping to 2566 and we end up being stuck in some kind of "loop" (instructions 2566, 2568, 256a, 256c are being executed repeatadly).

The instructions here are 2-byte sized (compressed), but while executing the `jal` instruction, the CPU saves `pc+4` instead of `pc+2` as a return address, just as if the executed instruction was 4-byte sized  (not compressed). For this reason I decided to rerun the simulation, but this time with a binary, that doesn't contain compressed instructions (remove `c` from `march` in https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/master/litex/soc/cores/cpu/cv32e41p/core.py#L32):
```
    "standard": "-march=rv32i2p0_m    -mabi=ilp32 ",
```
 After this change everything worked fine - I got the bios prompt.

(reading some issues related to OpenHW group cores)

@panantoni01 Hum, strange...
Does it mean there would be a bug with compressed instructions on the 41P?
I haven't seen issues related to it in the openhwgroup repository... :neutral_face:

Thanks for the report and the detailed analysis.

I integrated a workaround/fix in cbac44ac3:
  cpu/cv32e41p: Avoid compressed codegen by default

The issue appears to come from firmware being built with RV32IMC by default. In the failing trace, a compressed `jal` stores `pc+4` instead of `pc+2` as the return address, which skips the caller return-address restore and leaves the BIOS stuck in a loop.

The CV32E41P `standard` variant now builds LiteX software as RV32IM, so GCC will not emit compressed instructions by default. I also kept the previous RV32IMC behavior available  explicitly through the new `imc` variant for anyone wanting to debug or validate the compressed path.

I added a focused regression test for the advertised GCC flags. Full `litex_sim --cpu-type=cv32e41p` boot still needs validation in an environment with `pythondata-cpu-cv32e41p`  installed.

Update: this issue appears to be in the CV32E41P CPU RTL, not in the LiteX wrapper.

The failing case is compressed code, specifically a `c.jal` path where the link address can become `pc+4` instead of `pc+2`. That writes the wrong return address, skips the caller's  `ra` restore, and then execution loops.

The root cause I found is that the RTL computes `is_compressed_o` in `cv32e41p_merged_decoder.sv`, but this signal is not declared as a decoder output port and is not connected in   `cv32e41p_id_stage.sv`. With permissive SystemVerilog handling, `id_stage_i.is_compressed` becomes an implicit undriven net, so the `IMMB_PCINCR` path can use the wrong increment.

The minimal CPU RTL patch that fixes the simulation is:

  ```diff
  diff --git a/rtl/cv32e41p_merged_decoder.sv b/rtl/cv32e41p_merged_decoder.sv
  @@
     input  logic [31:0] instr_rdata_i,
  +  output logic        is_compressed_o,

  diff --git a/rtl/cv32e41p_id_stage.sv b/rtl/cv32e41p_id_stage.sv
  @@
     logic is_clpx, is_subrot;
  +  logic is_compressed;
  @@
         .instr_rdata_i(instr),
  +      .is_compressed_o(is_compressed),
  ```

With this patch, cv32e41p/imc boots in LiteX simulation. However, since the upstream CV32E41P repository is archived, we cannot upstream the CPU RTL fix cleanly. So on the LiteX side  we will keep CV32E41P on the known-good standard RV32IM variant and avoid advertising an imc variant.
This is done with https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/d86a229ea95b70a9c50d914adb28f03205abdd12 and cv32e41p is now also tested back in ci.

title: axi-lite CSR `.we` not obeying single-cycle interface spec
body:
According to:

https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/937428b1fc3953bdc1726f292f4cb9bb163bf5cd/litex/soc/interconnect/csr.py#L98-L108

The `.re` and `.we` signals should pulse high for exactly one cycle. However, in practice, I am finding that on an `axi-lite` system, the `.we` signal stays high for longer than one cycle. 

I am using the following simple test bench to create CSRs that exercise the corner cases:

```python

            # test that caching is OFF for the I/O regions
            self.sim_coherence_w = CSRStorage(32, name= "wdata", description="Write values here to check cache coherence issues")
            self.sim_coherence_r = CSRStatus(32, name="rdata", description="Data readback derived from coherence_w")
            self.sim_coherence_inc = CSRStatus(32, name="rinc", description="Every time this is read, the base value is incremented by 3", reset=0)

            self.sync += [
                If(self.sim_coherence_inc.we,
                    self.sim_coherence_inc.status.eq(self.sim_coherence_inc.status + 3)
                ).Else(
                    self.sim_coherence_inc.status.eq(self.sim_coherence_inc.status)
                )
            ]
            self.comb += [
                self.sim_coherence_r.status.eq(self.sim_coherence_w.storage + 5)
            ]
```

This is connected to a system that uses an axi-lite bus via a crossbar framework that uses axi, so the overall connectivity is CPU (axi4) -> crossbar (axi4) -> AXI2Axilite -> Axilite2Simple -> CSR banks.

Basically, the test bench will "add 3" to `rinc` every time it is read, so successive reads should generate a series of numbers like 0, 3, 6, 9, ...

This is what I'm seeing in practice:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1168375/205859545-081364de-9c83-4506-aa75-c05043181d72.png)

The `.we` signal stays selected for much more than one cycle, so the register increments more than it should.

The `.we` signal seems this is derived from this code:

https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/937428b1fc3953bdc1726f292f4cb9bb163bf5cd/litex/soc/interconnect/csr_bus.py#L183-L198

The `sel` comes from just checking that the address matches, and is then applied with the `If(sel, Case(...))` in the final `sync` section at the bottom. Thus it's assumed that the address provided on the bus should be valid for exactly one cycle to create a one-cycle wide `.we` pulse.

However, the address is applied for multiple cycles. The AXI->Axilite and back again conversion can't complete in a single cycle, so the address is asserted for multiple cycles as the whole round-trip completes.

I'm guessing this bug may not have been noticed because not many systems trigger errors if a CSR is read from multiple times. In practice I don't have any blocks that break if this spec is violated, but, I would really like the axi-lite CSR implementation to behave spec-identical to the wishbone stuff, it would make me sleep better at night.

That being said, I am running into myriad issues trying to rework the system to obey this discipline. There are issues both in the Axi2Axilite converter, and also in the CSR interface itself. The Axi2Axilite converter is issuing two cycles for every one AXI request, and the CSR interface behavior doesn't match what's expected of AXI due to a mismatch in cycle delays, so the fix isn't simple.

I'll open a PR to address this issue but all my code also depends on PR #1506 being accepted, since I can't run simulations without it.

body:
The `.bat` file generated on Windows is invalid. Contents of the file are:
```
@echo off
rem Autogenerated by LiteX / git: cb85a8ca

yosys -l colorlight_5a_75e.rpt colorlight_5a_75e.ys

 || exit /becppack  --bootaddr 0   --compress  colorlight_5a_75e.config --svf colorlight_5a_75e.svf --bit colorlight_5a_75e.bit  || exit /b
```

Problem is are the lines starting witg `||`, I think this should be formatted on the previous line.

The commands themselves are correct, as I can copy them to the command line and build the firmware.

I'm using the latest version of Litex. Thanks for this great project!

comments.body:
The problem lays in, amongst others, in the file `litex/build/yosys_wrapper.py`. Here the command is created and the string is terminated by a new-line character, i.e.:
```
base_cmd = f"yosys -l {self._build_name}.rpt {self._build_name}.ys\n"
```

In `litex/build/yosys_nextpnr_toolchain.py` the fail-statement is added using string concatenation, so that will end up on the next line. This only affects Windows, because for Linux does not use `fail_stmt` at this moment.

To solve this issue, there are two possible solutions:

1.  Not terminating the commands with `\n`, but leave that to the `build_script` function. This means all functions for commands have to be checked (not only the yosys+nextpnr-ecp5 toolchain I use.
2.  In the `build_script` command use `.rstrip` to strip all white-space (including newlines) from the command. 

I would recommend to go for the second option. In that case the function would look like this:
```python
...
        # yosys call
        script_contents += f"{self._yosys.get_yosys_call('script').rstrip()} {fail_stmt\n"
        # nextpnr call
        script_contents += f"{self._nextpnr.get_call('script').rstrip()} {fail_stmt}\n"
...
```

If you want I can make a PR.
Hi, true `\n` are not correctly uses: [PR](https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/pull/1537) triy to fix this error.
Could you try it to validates this PR fixes your issue?

This should already be fixed by #1537 / d17041e07.

The issue was that the Yosys/nextpnr wrapper commands already contained newlines, while the Windows `|| exit /b` failure handler was appended afterwards, causing invalid `.bat` output. The wrappers now  return command strings without trailing newlines and the build script generation adds the failure handler/newline in one place.

So this should be resolved on current `master`. If it can still be reproduced with current LiteX, please share the generated `.bat` file and the exact target/toolchain command. Otherwise I think we can close this.

Related issue:
Meson build doesn't seem to work with the new RISC-V GCC tool chain.
```
../../../pythondata-software-picolibc/pythondata_software_picolibc/data/meson.build:35:0: ERROR: Value "c18" (of type "string") for combo option "C language standard to use" is not one of the choices. Possible choices are (as string): "none", "c89", "c99", "c11", "gnu89", "gnu99", "gnu11".
```
Do I have the wrong one on the path?

> Tools don't like the new Meson Release Dec 23.

https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/e8322587a06f2f3e82443cc6422ba230b11c195a/litex/soc/integration/builder.py#L256-L266

This seems like a pretty odd check to me. It's checking to see if the major version is older than 0, OR if the minor version is older than 59.

Checking the major version doesn't even make *sense*, the minimum requirement here is "0".

Anyway, this check is definitely not a real version comparison. It should use a version tuple instead:

```python
if tuple(int(i) for i in meson_version[:3]) < (0, 59, 0):
         msg = f"Meson version too old. Found ......."
```

Because it's not an either-or.

You could also do this:
```meson
from packaging.version import Version

meson_version = Version(subprocess.check_output(["meson", "-v"]).decode("utf-8"))

if meson_version < Version('0.59.0'):
    msg = f"Meson version too old. Found ......."
```

That does require the https://pypi.org/project/packaging/ module, which is reasonably common at least. It also guarantees proper "version specifiers" support.
The new `apt install riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc` default to gcc 7.5 which causes the second meson error listed above.
Google colab uses Ubuntu 18 and therefore only installs the riscv64 gcc 7.5.  I had to manually install the newer RISCV binaries.

body:
When mapping data to the X-HEEP data_flash_only section as in [this example](https://github.com/esl-epfl/x-heep/blob/main/sw/applications/example_spi_write/main.c#L236), the test fails as the values read back are all 0s.

By adding printf here and there in `iceprog`, I could see data being written correctly from the compiled `.hex` file.
Even when such `.hex` file gets modified by hand.

I noticed that the data written are above the file_size, as this does not take into account gaps into the address space.
by adding a "+1" [here](https://github.com/esl-epfl/x-heep/blob/main/sw/vendor/yosyshq_icestorm/iceprog/iceprog.c#L1014) 

```
for (int addr = begin_addr; addr < end_addr+1; addr += block_size) {
```

I erased one extra 64KB block to be sure to erase also data above the address that I wanted to write.

The values are mapped at address 0x10000, and `printf` into the `flash_prog` functions show that data are written as expected, and `printf` in the `flash_read` functions confirm that the data read are correct.

When running on X-HEEP instead, `prinft` into the `bsp` functions show that the address and data written are correct, but when reading, only values equal to `0` are read, failing the test.

title: Remove trailing commas in hjson files
body:
Hjson files should not contain commas at the end of each line.  In particular, they MUST NOT in the case of "quoteless strings".  However, the use of these commas is widespread in X-HEEP, which results in incorrect Hjson files.

Quoting [the Hjson documentation](https://hjson.github.io/syntax.html):

> ### Quoteless Strings
> [...]
> **Do not** add **commas** or comments as they would become part of the string.

Furthermore (although less importantly):

> ### Commas
> [...]
> You **should** omit **optional** commas [*other than for quoteless strings*] to make your data more readable.
> ```
> {
>   one: 1
>   two: 2
> }
> ```

However, there are plenty of Hjson files in X-HEEP that use trailing commas, which in many cases are illegal since they will be included as part of the string.  The most common cases are "barewords" and hex values starting with `0x` (which are actually strings, not numbers):
```
active:  low,
address: 0x10000000,
```
But I would just remove all the trailing commas, since they're entirely optional (when they're allowed) and the standard itself recommends removing them.  This includes trailing commas after a `],` or a `},`.

This issue seems to have been "fixed" in some places of the Python code by explicitly adding `.strip(',')`, but this is a workaround that "fixes the symptom" rather than fixing the broken file.  This can be problematic in a future; I recommend fixing all the .hjson files so that they're compliant with Hjson in this regard.

title: Remove unused clock from KCU105 example design's clock constraints
body:
The async clock declaration for the KCU105 example design is currently: 
```
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks sysclk] -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ infra/eth/phy/*/rxoutclk*}]] -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ txoutclk*}]]
```
This works well in Vivado 2016.4. However, it causes the following error during implementation with Vivado 2017.4:
```
[Vivado 12-4739] set_clock_groups:No valid object(s) found for '-group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ infra/eth/phy/*/rxoutclk*}]]'. 
```

In Vivado 2016.4, the expression `[get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ infra/eth/phy/*/rxoutclk*}]]` evaluates to ` infra/eth/phy/U0/pcs_pma_block_i/transceiver_inst/gig_ethernet_pcs_pma_basex_156_25_gt_i/inst/rxoutclk_out[0]`. However, when building with Vivado 2017.4 a newer version of the Ethernet IP core is used, and that clock no longer exists in the design; in contrast, all the design's other clocks (there's 5) remain the same from 2016.4 to 2017.4.

Deeper inspection reveals that 2016.4 builds this clock is not used for any paths, and so it can be safely removed from the async clock constraints declaration. The new declaration should be:
```
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks sysclk] -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ txoutclk*}]]
```

title: Cache performance will degrade in some simulator due to the implement of module "cache_lru"
body:
Recently I have managed to port the Nyuzi to Xilinx ZC706 evaluation board and run doom & quakeview successfully, with respect. But during this process, I noticed a cache performance degradation when debugging with Modelsim SE 10.5c. Since such degradation seems only existing when simulating in some simulators and doesn't exist in verilator or after synthesize, I think maybe this topic is more like a portability suggestion than an issue.

When running the core on some simulators such as Modelsim, the x value coming from uninitialized SRAM will cause the casez statement in module cache_lru fail to match any pattern, further cause that in all cache set only way 0 is available. To illustrate it clearly, here is a piece of code snipping from cache_lru.sv when parameter NUM_WAYS is 4.

```
...

#130            4:
#131            begin
#132                always_comb
#133                begin
#134                    casez (lru_flags)
#135                        3'b00?: fill_way = 0;
#136                        3'b10?: fill_way = 1;
#137                        3'b?10: fill_way = 2;
#138                        3'b?11: fill_way = 3;
#139                        default: fill_way = '0;
#140                    endcase
#141                end
#142
#143                always_comb
#144                begin
#145                    case (new_mru)
#146                        2'd0: update_flags = {2'b11, lru_flags[0]};
#147                        2'd1: update_flags = {2'b01, lru_flags[0]};
#148                        2'd2: update_flags = {lru_flags[2], 2'b01};
#149                        2'd3: update_flags = {lru_flags[2], 2'b00};
#150                        default: update_flags = '0;
#151                    endcase
#152                end
#153            end

...
```

Consider after reset, two or more cache fill operations happened in the same cache set. When the first fill request comes, because the value of "lru_flags" is 3'bxxx (the value of uninitialized SRAM), the default branch will take effect, way 0 got filled, and the "update_flags" will be 3'b11x. Then, in the subsequent request handling process, the casez statement will always fail to match any pattern with the value of "lru_flags" (3'b11x), the default branch will always take effect, way 0 will always get filled, and "update_flags" will always be 3'b11x. The similar issue also exists when NUM_WAY is 8. The marked red area in the waveform generated by Modelsim attached below shows such situation:

![lru_waveform](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25722008/1ba40f0e-3145-11e7-93f3-f02092e1a397.png)

Although it sounds like a bad idea, one solution to this problem is changing all casez in cache_lru.sv to casex. I made an experiment to estimate the performance impact: Some logic was inserted into the writeback_stage firstly to trace the function activity. Then, the same program got executed on two different designs, the original design and the design with modified cache_lru, for a given time. Since the program is same, the amount of log generated during simulation is related to the instructions got executed. By comparing the number of function tracing record, we can compare the performance approximately. The screenshot below shows the result: The design with modified cache_lru produced 2.8x more log than the original one, which can roughly be considered as running faster 2.8x.

![log](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25721242/4dfccdae-3142-11e7-8a54-6c918b5deaa7.png)

The version I use is ce221ff, but this issue still exists in the latest version.

Finally, Thanks for bringing such interesting project!

![img_20170502_233302](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25722013/219d087a-3145-11e7-8ea3-75685d58b288.jpg)

comments.body:

title: Floating point addition overflow handled incorrectly

comments.body:
Test case here:
https://github.com/jbush001/NyuziProcessor/blob/0abeff4141498d58524fb742c454572bc1d23d54/tests/core/isa/float.S#L78

The operands have an exponent of 0xfe, which is the maximum allowable value for a non-special floating point value. When the significands are added together, the result is one bit larger, so it is shifted right one and one is added to the exponent here:

https://github.com/jbush001/NyuziProcessor/blob/dd399787f91cbbdaaf9791e4ace6b2d37423531e/hardware/core/fp_execute_stage5.sv#L100

As a result, the result exponent becomes 0xff, which is a special. Because the significand is non-zero, this represents NaN. It should be inf, which has a zero significand. I think the right thing to do is reuse the special logic here:

https://github.com/jbush001/NyuziProcessor/blob/dd399787f91cbbdaaf9791e4ace6b2d37423531e/hardware/core/fp_execute_stage5.sv#L115

and add an additional case that checks for the exponent becoming too large.

fix_commits.messageHeadline: Issue #124 JTAG test intermittently fails with incorrect value

comments.body: There is a race condition. In the cycle the debug unit asserts its halt, the instruction fetch tag stage requests an instruction. The next cycle, the instruction fetch data logic sees a valid instruction and attempts to issue to the next stage: ```SystemVerilog ifd_instruction_valid <= (ift_instruction_requested && !rollback_this_stage && cache_hit && ift_tlb_hit && !alignment_fault) || (dbg_instruction_inject_en && core_selected_debug); ``` However, the mux is now pulling an instruction from the debug unit, which is some uninitialized garbage value: ```SystemVerilog assign ifd_instruction = dbg_halt ? dbg_instruction_inject : {fetched_word[7:0], fetched_word[15:8], fetched_word[23:16], fetched_word[31:24]}; ``` This is a multi-cycle vector load, which eventually hangs because the jtag unit can't restart the instruction.
Tested this by running JTAG test 100 times in a row. Didn't see the failure (which was fairly common before).

title: Assertion when interrupt occurs during synchronized store
body:
This occurred in the io_interrupt test:

```
io_interrupt
Process returned error: Random seed is 1460932741
cores 1|threads per core 4|l1i$ 16k 4 ways|l1d$ 16k 4 ways|l2$ 128k 8 ways|itlb 64 entries|dtlb 64 entries
>ABC*DE*FGHI*JKLM*NOPQ*RSTU*VWXYZ*abcd*efgh*ijklm*nopq*rstu*vwxy*z0123*4567*89
[32128] %Error: l1_store_queue.sv:208: Assertion failed in TOP.v.nyuzi.core_gen[0].core.l1_l2_interface.l1_store_queue.thread_store_buf_gen[0]
%Error: core/l1_store_queue.sv:208: Verilog $stop
```

The code is here:

``` systemverilog
                    if (store_requested_this_entry)
                    begin
                        if (is_restarted_sync_request)
                        begin
                            ...
                            assert(!rollback[thread_idx]);    // <----- Here
```

The problem appears to be as follows:
1. Core initiates synchronized store. The first instruction issue is rolled back and the state is recorded in  the synchronized flag in the store buffer entry.
2. Interrupt occurs and thread is rolled back.
3. The interrupt handler attempts to do a store (of any type) before the response comes back for the synchronized store request.
4. In l1_store_queue, is_restarted_sync_request will be true because there is already a store with the synchronized flag set. The logic assumes this is the restarted synchronized store request. However, rollback will be set to 1 for this thread because the entry is still pending and can_write_combine is 0. 

l1_store_queue assumes a core will not attempt to issue another store after it's been rolled back until the l1_store_queue wakes it:

``` verilog
     else if (pending_stores[thread_idx].valid && !can_write_combine
         && !got_response_this_entry)
         rollback[thread_idx] = 1;
```

The reason it occurred in this test was  because there is a spinlock in crt0.s when the program terminates (for calling destructors). A compiler update changed the timing enough to hit this race condition. A better test would be to issue synchronized stores in a loop with interrupts enabled.

The fix is probably to disable interrupts while a synchronized store is pending. Something similar is already done for I/O operations: the ic_interrupt_pending bitmask goes into the instruction_decode_state to detect this stage. An additional signal could go from the store buffer to indicate this.

title: The very first Ethernet frame after reset never leaves the device?
body:
While continuing to investigate network startup time (and https://github.com/FreeRTOS/FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP/issues/1244 in particular), I found what looks like it might be a hardware or driver bug that's beyond my present understanding.  _Specifically, it looks like the Ethernet block fails to send the very first packet it's given._  I am unsure if this is an IP block issue or a driver issue (perhaps we're failing to wait long enough for autonegotiation or link training or somesuch?).  This appears to happen on both warm (`mem_helper.sh`) and cold (power cycle and `mem_helper.sh`) resets of the Sonata.

Turning several debugging knobs up to 11 and adding a few more informative `printf`s, the system spews forth:

* Initialization:
  ```
  Ethernet driver: Acknowledged interrupt, sleeping on futex 0x10bf04 (v:1 0x10bf04-0x10bf08 l:0x4 o:0x0 p: G R----- -- ---)
  vDHCPProcessEndPoint: enter 0
  DHCP-socket[fe-7a]: DHCP Socket Create
  prvCreateDHCPSocket[fe-7a]: open, user count 1
  prvInitialiseDHCP: start after 25 ticks
  vDHCP_RATimerReload: 25
  vDHCPProcessEndPoint: exit 1
  ```

* Attempt to send a DHCP Discover packet without the broadcast-reply flag set (`xUseBroadcast=0`):
  ```
  vDHCPProcessEndPoint: enter 1
  nwf prvSendDHCPDiscover from xHandleWaitingFirstDiscover

title: CJALR with instr[14:12] != 0 is not illegal
body:
The decoder for CJALR will not raise an illegal instruction exception when `instr[14:12] != 0`, but it will also not set `cheri_jalr_en`:

https://github.com/microsoft/cheriot-ibex/blob/3f0ec8600cb7621c4c952951d211b3515116ea27/rtl/ibex_decoder.sv#L343-L367

When a CJALR instruction is run with `instr[14:12] != 0`, the instruction that runs becomes one which stores the next instruction PC to the register file, but does not branch, since it runs into the old logic for JALR. This is therefore not a security issue, but is a bug.

Instead `illegal_insn` should be set when `instr[14:12] != 0` (see the original code for JALR, which does the same).

I agree, this is bug indeed. Will fix, thanks.

title: Instruction Fetch failing when the Sail doesn't
body:
Currently the IF stage will incorrectly raise a fetch error exception in the following two cases:
1. The instruction is uncompressed and the PC is`2**32 - 2`, meaning the instruction wraps around the address space, but the PCC allows execution anywhere. This is allowed by the Sail because it checks the two two byte chunks of the instruction separately.
2. The PC is `0` and `PCC.top33 = 2**32`. This fails because `PCC.top33 - 0` still has the top bit set, even though no overflow occurred. This is easily fixed by updating `cheri_bound_vio` to
```
assign cheri_bound_vio = /* snip */ || (instr_hdrm[32] & (|if_instr_addr)) || ~hdrm_ok;
```

The first case is very minor, especially since the RTL is being stricter (not weaker) than the Sail. One could update the RTL to do both checks separately, or update the Sail to do one the one check.

Less ideally, because we know the RTL is stricter than the Spec in a very specific and documentable way I could just allow it in the verification setup and essentially relax the constraint to be at least as strict, instead of identical to. Again, I would obviously prefer not to do this.

fix_commits.messageHeadline: added handling for pc wraparound case in if_stage (issue #34)

RTL commit [4a739b4](https://github.com/microsoft/cheriot-ibex/commit/4a739b4f4bcf0324633ba4d7a0286fa6dfd9a04f) fixed issue #2 (PC=0, top33=0x10000_0000) by extending the math to 34 bit.
I can confirm that your fix did fix the second issue. Are you intending to fix the first or should I close this issue?
Thanks, let's keep this open for now.

@mndstrmr , I checked in an RTL fix ([2a0c157](https://github.com/microsoft/cheriot-ibex/commit/2a0c1570bf63b9cb20fe4248ca5792a2614c97a8)) by adding the allow_all condition (pcc top33/base32 covers the entire address space). I think it should make it match sail behavior now - please verify. thanks.

There is currently a bug in exception priorities in Ibex.  See [this comment](https://github.com/microsoft/cheriot-rtos/blob/94dca15276348727ff6ffccbafb2c2be91aafe98/sdk/include/fail-simulator-on-error.h#L61) for the work-around that we use in the software stack. You might be interested in talking to Tom Melham at Oxford.  His students have been working on verifying the Ibex.

Any way you can attach your ibex trace for the exception handler execution? Quoting your reply on #111 (to keep the msleep discussion in one thread):

> I haven't had time to look at your work yet, but regarding the msleep issue, there's one thing I would check first. Not sure if this is the problem, but you can e.g. check the compiled zephyr.lst and see if there are any mul operations present.

I first tried on v2.4.0 and ran into the MUL bug. Without any fix (i.e. with "illegal" MULs in the binary), `k_msleep` sleeps for zero time (returns immediately), with your fix from https://github.com/olofk/serv/issues/102#issuecomment-1667263644, it shows the same behavior as vanilla 3.5.0. I haven't checked that there are really no more MULs present. I can look into that in the upcoming days just to make sure.

I checked now with 2.4.0 and I can reproduce the issue. TBH, I never really understood how this timer API is supposed to work, so there's a fair chance I'm doing something strange but I can't see what it is right away. Will need some debugging. In case you haven't seen already, you can run with `--trace_pc` and `--vcd` to dump the PC and waveform of all signals respectively.

Ooooh nice, thanks for the tips with debugging this. I'll see whether I can figure something out. (I'll probably get to it only next weekend though.)

I think I found the issue. `sys_clock_driver_init` (formerly `z_clock_driver_init') is never called. I added the corresponding macro as part of my v3.5.0 PR.

diff --git a/zephyr/drivers/timer/serv_timer.c b/zephyr/drivers/timer/serv_timer.c

```

I haven't verified that the timing checks out yet though.

Well spotted! I'll do a proper review of #111 as soon as I can
Cool, thanks!

Oh oh, actually it's not quite fixed yet. After running the design for a few minutes (~10 minutes is enough, probably less), the application freezes again. Probably something to do with the timer overflowing. I haven't had the time to look at the code yet though.

I think this is a problem in the Verilog timer. Take the following example which resets the Verilog timer close to its overflow value (and adds some debugging):

```diff
diff --git a/servant/servant_timer.v b/servant/servant_timer.v
index 45306e9..656c1cd 100644
--- a/servant/servant_timer.v
+++ b/servant/servant_timer.v
@@ -23,15 +23,21 @@ module servant_timer

+   always @(posedge o_irq) begin

-      if (i_wb_cyc & i_wb_we)
+      if (i_wb_cyc & i_wb_we) begin
 	mtimecmp <= i_wb_dat[HIGH:0];
+        $display("set irq = 0x%x", i_wb_dat[HIGH:0]);
+      end
       mtime <= mtime + 'd1;
       o_irq <= (mtimeslice - mtimecmp >= 0);
       if (RESET_STRATEGY != "NONE")
 	if (i_rst) begin
-	   mtime <= 0;
-	   mtimecmp <= 0;
+	   mtime <= 4293916296;
+	   mtimecmp <= 4293916296;
 	end
    end
 endmodule
```

If you then run my loopy `hello_world`, you get:

```
make: Nothing to be done for 'all'.
Loading RAM from /home/markus/workspace/hello.hex
IRQ @0xffeff688 | 0xffeff688

set irq = 0x00059a00

set irq = 0x00062380

set irq = 0x0006b340
set irq = 0x0006b340
set irq = 0x00074300
set irq = 0x00074300
set irq = 0x0007d2c0
set irq = 0x0007d2c0
set irq = 0x00086280
set irq = 0x00086280
[... many more, they are printed immediately, IRQ is permanently active]
```

PS: I think #109 was supposed to address this, but I do not see how this makes a difference. Example 4-bit timer, max count 15.

* IRQ! We are at count 13. -> We set the next cmp to 4
* Verilog does 13 - 4 = 9, which is greater than zero -> next interrupt fires immediately. 

Without having thought it through, wouldn't the following be the proper fix (and even reduce logic):

* `mtime` always increments 1 (no change)
* if `mtime` == `mtimecmp` -> set IRQ (compare equal, set latching IRQ flag)
* if write to bus -> reset IRQ and update mtimecmp (reset latch on bus access)

OR: As a more extreme alternative, change the timer to a self-resetting kind when it reaches cmp (auto retrigger). Advantage: In a tickful kernel, we wouldn't have to do any math in the IRQ (which is important, because there are divisions and multiplications!) Disadvantage: I'll have to check, but we might lose support of tickless kernels, but I'm not sure.

Good debugging! Yes, #109 was supposed to fix this, but in hindsight I should definitely have checked myself that it worked correctly. I don't have any strong opinions on what kind of timer we want to have. The idea was to have a 32-bit timer, but otherwise follow the RISC-V machine timer as closely as possible to make the software support easier. Not sure if I succeeded in that. I agree there's an alarming number of math operations in the IRQ handler, and avoiding those sounds like a good idea. And I'm not sure I understand the implications of a tickless kernel, tbh. Power savings seems to be one thing, but there might be other benefits as well?

A third option could be to just implement a proper 64-bit RISC-V machine timer instead. It will cost a little bit more, but since it's an optional feature outside of the CPU, it's not the end of the world. The 2018 SoftCPU contest is already over by now and that was really the main reason for keeping down the size of the whole SoC.

I can think of a couple of different strategies. One would be to bisect between 2.4 and 3.5 to figure out where it stops working. Or did you say it's not working with 2.4 either? It sucks if we need to wait ten minutes for it to display the problem.

Another way would be to compare the soc support files in serv with the ones upstream and see if there is some issue there.

Replacing the serv_timer with a real risc-v machine timer is probably also a good idea to avoid having to carry our own driver. I started working on that a bit. Will push something later. Also just pushed a branch with some helpful debug registers to make troubleshooting with waveforms slightly less awful https://github.com/olofk/serv/tree/dbg

As noted in PR #111 (https://github.com/olofk/serv/pull/111#issuecomment-1847374609), this problems seems to be related to the toolchain emitting invalid MUL instructions (as part of picolibc, even if disabled), breaking the timing calculations. The driver and Verilog appears to be fine.

title: [BUG] Instruction fetch misaligned exception raised when a conditional branch that is not taken
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Hi,

According to the RISC-V 2.2 specification p.11: 
> An instruction address misaligned exception is generated on a taken branch or unconditional jump if the target address is not four-byte aligned. **No instruction fetch misaligned exception is generated for a conditional branch that is not taken**

But in `core/branch_unit.sv`, the exception is raised in branch unit as long as target address is misaligned *without taking the conditional branch result into account* :
`if (branch_valid_i && target_address[0] != 1'b0) branch_exception_o.valid = 1'b1;` from [line 94](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/72143ef0a9b50f2aaffa708a55263a5971bf0354/core/branch_unit.sv#L94) 

The fix should augment the `if` condition to include condition check that validate it is either an unconditional jump  or a **taken** conditional branch.


Thanks!

title: [Possible Issue] Non-selectable address matching mode leads to an incorrect PMP configuration update
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Instruction execution field `X`, and probably others, of PMP configuration CSRs is not updated correctly when trying to write non-selectable address matching value of field `A` in case PMP granularity `G` is `1`. Is this intended?

### RISC-V Specification
Unprivileged ISA: [20191213](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1s0lZxUZaa7eV_O0_WsZzaurFLLww7ou5/view) | Privileged Architecture: [20211203](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1EMip5dZlnypTk7pt4WWUKmtjUKTOkBqh/view) | External Debug Support: [0.13.02](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1XSPqW3WIfflIMeuGJBxGTMOEyeuRAQ5F/view)
> The PMP configuration registers are densely packed into CSRs to minimize context-switch time.
For RV32, sixteen CSRs, pmpcfg0–pmpcfg15, hold the configurations pmp0cfg–pmp63cfg for the 64
PMP entries, as shown in Figure 3.31.

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/09e7e476-c3a1-40c0-8a69-e2a59804d6f5)

> Figure 3.35 shows the layout of a PMP configuration register. The R, W, and X bits, when set,
indicate that the PMP entry permits read, write, and instruction execution, respectively. When
one of these bits is clear, the corresponding access type is denied. The R, W, and X fields form a
collectiveWARL field for which the combinations with R=0 and W=1 are reserved. The remaining
two fields, A and L, are described in the following sections.

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/ca0ef0fb-261a-4e5d-a7ca-577121aa18ac)

> The A field in a PMP entry’s configuration register encodes the address-matching mode of the
associated PMP address register.

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/ec536bae-9b3f-4c48-90d4-4b555cf78c8e)

> Although the PMP mechanism supports regions as small as four bytes, platforms may specify
coarser PMP regions. In general, the PMP grain is 2G+2 bytes and must be the same across all
PMP regions. When G ≥ 1, the NA4 mode is not selectable.


### Example Scenario

As shown below, the following sequence of instructions happens: 
> CSRRS x0, pmp_cfg0, x1

The instruction `CSRRS x0, pmp_cfg0, x1` is decoded at `t_id` and executed in machine mode resulting in updating the architecture state at `t_arch_update`. As a result, instruction execution field `X` of `pmp3cfg` is not updated as expected. Where it's supposed to be set according to the written value of `x1`. Probably the reason for that is trying to write `NA4` value to the `A` field of the same register `pmp3cfg`, which is not selectable when the granularity `G` is `1`, and thus updating `A` is ignored correctly, but `X` has to be updated correctly still!

title: [BUG] Wrong exception cause being raised in CSR Logic (illegal instruction instead of Virtual Instruction exception)
[BUG] An exploitable Meltdown vulnerability was found in CVA6
body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ### Bug Description Hi! Our processor side-channel vulnerability detection work has found an efficient and fault-tolerant Meltdown vulnerability on CVA6, which allows an attacker to leak kernel-space data at arbitrary addresses from user space. This vulnerability takes advantage of the feature of the CVA6 scoreboard: in-flight intructions in the scoreboard won’t trigger exceptions until they commit. Thus, we can access privilege data in a transient execution window and encode the privileged data in the microarchitecture. We provide an end-to-end exploit code and vulnerability explanation below. ```asm 2f40: fdiv.d fa5,fa5,fa4 2f44: lb t1, 0(a0) # a0 contains secret address 0xffffffffffe06f30, secret data is 0x30 2f48: slli t1, t1, 5 # encode secret to a probe array (index = secret << 5, t1 = 0x30 << 5 = 0x600) 2f4c: add t0, t1, t0 # encode secret to a probe array (base = 0x10000, t0 = base + t1 = 0x10600) 2f50: ld t1, 0(t0) # encode the secret to cache ``` The code runs under U-mode. The `lb` at `0x2f44` tries to access `0xffffffffffe06f30`, which is a kernel-space address. After the secret data is loaded, it will be encoded into the cache through the user-space array with the base address of `0x10000`. Due to the long latency of `fdiv` and the function [unit ready status](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L413), subsequent instructions will be issued during the `fdiv` transition execution window, as the waveform shows. **G1** represents the commit signals, **G2** represents scoreboard entries and **G3** represents the LSU, Dcache and memory bus behaviors. The first `lsu_valid_i` is triggered by `lb`, and the access address is successfully translated. The secret data is read from the Dcache and forwarded to the scoreboard. Thus, the `slli` and `add` can be issued in sequence. Finally, the secret is encoded in `t0`, which is the load address of` ld` at `0x2f50`. This is a cache-miss address. Thus, Dcache will fill the cacheline by initiating a memory access, as observed in `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`. All of the above processes take place within the `fdiv` transient execution window. In fact, when executing the `lb` at `0x2f44` architecturally, a load page fault exception will be triggered, and `t1` result will be 0. However, this is not important. We have already encoded the secret in the microarchitecture. Then we try to probe whether we successfully encoded the secret into the cache. The code sequentially accessed the memory addresses `0x105e0`, `0x10600`, `0x10620`, and `0x10640`. These addresses belong to different cachelines. ```asm probe: li t0, 0x10600 2f7c: ld t1, -32(t0) # cache miss 2f80: ld t1, 0(t0) # cache hit, addr = 0x10000 + 0x30 << 5 2f84: ld t1, 32(t0) # cache miss 2f88: ld t1, 64(t0) # cache miss ``` As shown in the waveform, compared with the `ld` that accesses `0x10600`, all the other `ld` have significantly longer execution times and all exhibit bus memory access behavior. Therefore, through the time side-channel, we can recover the aforementioned secret data. It is worth noting that this vulnerability has a high level of **fault tolerance**. Even if the secret address results in a TLB miss, this transient window is long enough to complete the Page Table Walk process. Similarly, if the address of the probe array also results in a TLB miss, the Page Table Walk can still be completed, and the secret can be encoded in the TLB. This vulnerability can be reproduced at the master commit aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd and the default cv64a6_imafdc_sv39 config. The full elf file are provided below. [rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24147141/rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip)

title: [BUG] Out-of-Order Not Working
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

## Bug Explanation

I noticed the docs say that Out-of-Order can occur between the multiplier and the ALU, however this is not the case according to the RTL.

Docs:

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/a29b231070f2dccca53eae2681120116633a4ffc/docs/03_cva6_design/issue_stage.md?plain=1#L42-L54

RTL:

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/adf99b53042d2b14cbbb36689babf8cd4c03cf81/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L135-L152

For example, I have this code snippet:

```
        div     t2, t0, t1
        fsqrt.s f1, f1
        lw      t5, 0(s1)
        add     t6, t0, t1
```

And this is it's execute stage:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/43790149/223483191-73f6885e-c1e1-4930-bf28-4377288d72b6.png)

As you can see, the `add` instruction isn't run until after the `div` finishes.

## Proposed Fix

Either:

* The RTL could be changed to separate the ALU and multiplier into two separate busy signals.
* The example in the docs could be changed to something else, such as `div` and `lsu`.

docs: fix example of OoO write-back to scoreboard (#1621)

comments.body: If you like, I can submit a pull request changing the docs to give div and lsu as the example

Hello @sifferman and thanks for opening this issue.

I had a look, I think I have found a too strict restriction (#1230) related to `mult -> *` sequences. However it does not seem to fix this issue about `div -> flu` sequences.

The parallelism is only possible for units spread on different result buses, so that their result can be provided to the scoreboard without conflicts. For the `div -> add` sequence you show, they use the same result bus (named `flu` as "fixed latency unit", even if div does not have a fixed latency), so you are right, the doc example is wrong.

A few suggestions/ideas:

- We can update the docs as you suggest.
- We could add a write-back port for `mult/div` but we won't as the area cost would be considerable!
- We can check if there is a minimal latency for div; if so, maybe we could issue a few other FLU instructions just after the `div` starts?
- Maybe we could modify how the div result is handled: when div result is available, if result bus is available then push the result, else store it in a (new?) register and lock the `flu` issues until the result bus is available, then release the lock and push the result.
- Maybe we could move the `mult/div` unit to the same port as FP operations?

Thanks for taking a look @cathales! I agree with your observations.

Actually, I believe that the throughput could increase quite a bit if the mult/div unit uses the FP port. On a mult/div instruction, it's probably more likely that the next instruction will be an ALU instruction than a FPU instruction. But I'm not sure how big of an endeavor it would be to complete this.

I will have time to look into it in about a month if progress hasn't been made on it sooner

If we move mult/div to FP port, I hope multiply-accumulate would not need bubbles anymore if the compiler is smart enough to avoid RAW hasards like below:

```asm
mul m0, a, b
; begin repeat
mul m1, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m0 ; now: bubble because same bus than previous mul -> after modification: issue ok
mul m0, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m1 ; bubble -> issue ok
; end repeat
add r, r, m0 ; issue ok
```

However, if the compiler does not do that (see below), there will be the same bubbles anyway so the modification will not impact performance.

```asm
; begin repeat
mul m, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m ; bubble because needs m from mul above and mul duration is 2 cycles
; end repeat
````

> Actually, I believe that the throughput could increase quite a bit if the mult/div unit uses the FP port. On a mult/div instruction, it's probably more likely that the next instruction will be an ALU instruction than a FPU instruction. But I'm not sure how big of an endeavor it would be to complete this.

For CoreMark the increase would be less than 3%, but it depends of the application.

About area:

For a configuration with both F and M, we use an existing write-back port so it is okay.

For a configuration with M, without F, today there should not be a write-back port for FPU, so the muxes in the scoreboard could be cheap. If we add one port for the multiplier, it means that the muxes are big.

So maybe the performance vs area cost should be discussed.

title: [BUG] About four-byte alignment on target addresses of control transfer instructions (branch_unit.sv)
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Hi,
 
In `core/branch_unit.sv` the `branch_exception_o.valid` is raised high only if the branch/jump target address is not aligned **on a two-byte boundary** ([line 94](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/513bb91f823a18a6653a1685acd60408049c9c8f/core/branch_unit.sv#L94C8-L96C10) checks only the LSB). That is, it enforces only two-byte boundary check, and does not raise exception when target address of JAL/JALR is not four-byte aligned. 
However, in RISC-V 2.1 specification p.16 says "The JAL and JALR instructions can generate a misaligned instruction fetch exception if the target address is not aligned to a four-byte boundary."

If my understanding is correct, I think the fix may need to change the condition of [line 94](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/513bb91f823a18a6653a1685acd60408049c9c8f/core/branch_unit.sv#L94C8-L96C10) from. 
`if (branch_valid_i && target_address[0] != 1'b0) branch_exception_o.valid = 1'b1;` to   
`if (branch_valid_i && (target_address[1:0] != 2'b00)) branch_exception_o.valid = 1'b1;`

Thanks!

title: Previous privilege mode mstatus field MPP holds reserved value
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Previous privilege mode field, `MPP`, of `mstatus` or `sstatus` holds reserved value. The example where this applies to `sstatus` is not shown here.

### RISC-V Specification
Unprivileged ISA: [20191213](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1s0lZxUZaa7eV_O0_WsZzaurFLLww7ou5/view) | Privileged Architecture: [20211203](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1EMip5dZlnypTk7pt4WWUKmtjUKTOkBqh/view) | External Debug Support: [0.13.02](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1XSPqW3WIfflIMeuGJBxGTMOEyeuRAQ5F/view)
> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/b6ee3012-d5e7-4f99-94c9-0cb40737aa43)

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/20941d38-bc11-4436-96b2-8ae3dfcaf8c6)


### Example Scenario

As shown below, the following sequence of instructions happens: 
> CSRRW x2, mstatus, x9 -> CSRRCI x1, mstatus, 0

The instruction `CSRRW x2, mstatus, x9` is decoded at `t_id` and executed in machine mode resulting in updating the architecture state at `t_arch_update`. As a result, a wrong value of the `MPP` field of `mstatus` is read considering that it's a reserved one.

![Issue_12](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/15258d6e-f2f0-4933-a000-a6eb61514b9f)

### Steps to Reproduce

Git Hash: [de2e254c](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/commit/de2e254cd4c2d3e3a6d4def1652918e8f2535512) | TARGET_CFG: [cv32a6_imac_sv0](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/include/cv32a6_imac_sv0_config_pkg.sv) | VCD: [issue_12.zip](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/files/14826417/issue_12.zip)

comments.body:
Hello @Bill94l, thank you for reporting the issue.

I will take a look on it, and let you know.

As you can see, the write-back mode of the HPDcache is not yet officially supported on the CVA6 as there is no a corresponding configuration, so you may have some issues. But anyway, It should in principle work.

Ok, I diagnosed the issue but I did not yet fixed it. It is not a very simple one. It is an integration bug: hpdcache in WB mode within the CVA6.

It is a cache coherency issue between the Icache and the Dcache (HPDcache). The runtime in the v-tests (tests with virtual memory), modifies instruction segments. These modifications are done locally in the HPDcache (because of the write-back mode), and are not visible by the instruction cache unless the HPDcache is flushed (this is not required when in write-through mode because the memory is always updated on writes). The runtime explicitly does this using a fence.i instruction, but currently this instruction only requests an invalidation of the Icache with no flush of the Dcache.

I need to modify the CVA6 controller to issue a CMO flush operation to the HPDCache in case of a fence.i instruction, or find another clever way to keep both caches coherent... I have some ideas but I will think it over a little more.

You will need to be a little patient for this one.

Hi @Bill94l,

The fix is on its way. I have an opened Pull Request #2691 that fixes the coherency issue between the Icache and the Dcache when using the HPDcache in WB mode.

```
[DRC MDRV-1] Multiple Driver Nets: Net SoC_i/cpu_0/inst/i_cva6_wrapper/i_ariane/i_cva6/ex_stage_i/lsu_i/gen_mmu.i_cva6_mmu/i_dtlb/vaddr_vpn_match[0][1]_395[0] has multiple drivers: SoC_i/cpu_0/inst/i_cva6_wrapper/i_ariane/i_cva6/ex_stage_i/lsu_i/gen_mmu.i_cva6_mmu/i_dtlb/i___14_i_10/O, and SoC_i/cpu_0/inst/i_cva6_wrapper/i_ariane/i_cva6/ex_stage_i/lsu_i/gen_mmu.i_cva6_mmu/i_dtlb/i___14_i_11/O.
...
```

The issue comes from `cva6_tlb.sv` where `vaddr_vpn_match[i_gen][HYP_EXT]` is assigned twice:

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd/core/cva6_mmu/cva6_tlb.sv#L112-L113

and

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd/core/cva6_mmu/cva6_tlb.sv#L180-L182

I am not knowledgeable enough to know which one is preferable: first one is more generic if more page table levels are to be implemented, second is simpler to understand.
